objectives: Music has a steady beat you can feel
The beats keep coming at the same speed
You can count the beats in a bar

concept.title: Feel the beat before you read one
concept.body: Put a hand on the table and tap along to a song you know. That steady tap is the **pulse** — it keeps going whether or not anything is playing over the top of it, like a clock or a heartbeat. Every beat lasts the same length as the one before it. Music is grouped into short chunks called **bars**, and in most music each bar holds the same number of beats. Counting them is how you know where you are. You do not need to read anything yet: listen, tap, and count.

teach.smartTip: Tap first, count second. If you try to count before you feel the beat, you will lose it.
teach.didYouKnow: Musicians say a piece is in four when each bar holds four beats — the count comes before any symbol on the page.

theoryInSound.prompt: Play the two bars, then tap every beat you hear.

objectives: Music uses only seven letter names, A to G
After G the names start again at A
There is no note called H

concept.title: Seven letters, then round again
concept.body: Every note in music is named with one of seven letters: **A B C D E F G**. That is the whole set. When you reach G the names do not carry on to H — they start again at A, and keep going round for as long as the instrument does. Going the other way works the same: below A comes G. This is the single fact everything else in music reading is counted from, so it is worth knowing it forwards and backwards rather than only forwards.

teach.smartTip: Say the seven letters out loud in a circle — A B C D E F G A B C — until the jump from G back to A stops feeling like a jump.
teach.didYouKnow: The seven letters are far older than the stave. Musicians were naming notes A to G centuries before anyone drew five lines to put them on.

objectives: The white keys repeat the seven letters, over and over
The black keys come in groups of two and three
You find any white key from the black-key group beside it

concept.title: The black keys are the landmarks
concept.body: A keyboard looks like a wall of identical white keys, and it is not. Look at the black keys instead: they come in a repeating pattern of **two, then three**. That pattern is the map. **C** is the white key just left of every group of two, and **D** sits between those two. **F** is just left of every group of three. Once you can find C and F you can count to any other letter, because the white keys simply run A B C D E F G and round again, left to right. Nobody counts from the end of the keyboard — everybody uses the black keys.

teach.smartTip: Find the group of two black keys first, every time. C is immediately to its left, and everything else is a short count from there.
teach.didYouKnow: The two-and-three pattern is what lets a pianist play in the dark, and it is why the keyboard is the fastest way to see how far apart two notes are.

objectives: A stave is five lines and the four spaces between them
A note sits either ON a line or IN a space
Written music has two directions: up the page is pitch, left to right is time

concept.title: Five lines, and two directions
concept.body:
Written music sits on a **stave**: five lines, with four spaces between them. A note is either **on a line**, with the line running straight through the middle of it, or **in a space**, sitting in the gap. There is no third option.

The stave carries two different things at once, and telling them apart is the whole trick. **Up and down** the page is **pitch** — how high or low a note sounds. **Left to right** is **time** — the order you play things in, first to last. So a note higher up the page sounds higher, and a note further right happens later.

One caution about that first rule: it holds within a single **clef**. A clef is the symbol at the start of the stave, and its job is to fix a reference pitch so you know which line means what. Change the clef and the same line means a different note, so 'higher up means higher sound' is only safe to use while you stay in one clef. You will meet a second clef in Grade 1. The two directions do different jobs, and it is easy to mix them up. Up the page means a higher sound. Left to right means later in time. So the note further to the left is played first, however high or low it sits.

teach.smartTip: Ask one question at a time: first is it on a line or in a space, then how high does it sit. Trying to see both at once is what makes a stave look like a blur.
teach.didYouKnow: Staves have had four, six and even eleven lines at various points in history. Five became the standard, and it sits comfortably inside what the eye can take in at a glance.

objectives: Four note shapes, and the length each one is written as
An open notehead lasts longer than a filled one
A quaver may carry a tail, or be beamed to its neighbour

concept.title: The shape tells you how long
concept.body:
A note's **shape** tells you how long it is written to last, measured against the pulse you counted in lesson 1. There are four to start with.

A **semibreve** is an open notehead with no stem, written as four beats. A **minim** is an open notehead with a stem, written as two. A **crotchet** is a filled notehead with a stem, written as one beat — this is the one you have been tapping. A **quaver** is a filled notehead with a tail, written as half a beat.

Read the notehead first: **open notes are long, filled notes are short**. Then look for the stem and the tail.

One thing to watch. A quaver does not always carry a tail. When two or more quavers fall in the same beat they are usually joined by a thick line across their stems, called a **beam** — and a beamed pair is still two quavers. It is the same note value, drawn tidily.

These lengths are what each shape is *written* as. How long a note actually sounds is a separate question a performer answers.

teach.smartTip: Open or filled, then stem or no stem, then tail or beam. Three quick looks name any of the four.
teach.didYouKnow: The names are British. American musicians call the same four shapes a whole note, half note, quarter note and eighth note — which say the lengths out loud.
